featuredContent: This section summarizes what ASD is, how it's evaluated, common symptoms, and why early diagnosis/education is important in an understandable language. It is not a substitute for diagnosis and treatment; expert evaluation is required if suspected.

sections.title: What is Autism Spectrum Disorder?
sections.description: What ASD is, why it's called a “spectrum”, and its key features.
sections.content:
Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition related to brain development. In ASD, persistent difficulties in social communication and social interaction can be seen, along with restricted/repetitive behaviors and interests.

Why is it called a “spectrum”?
- The severity, appearance of symptoms, and the person's need for support vary greatly.
- Some individuals may be independent with less support in daily life, while others may require more intensive and structured support.

ASD can also be seen with sensory differences:
- There may be over- or under-sensitivity to stimuli such as sound, light, touch, smell.

Note: ASD is not a “personality” or “choice”; it is a condition related to the person's developmental profile. The goal is to support communication, learning, independence, and quality of life.

sections.title: How is Autism Spectrum Disorder Classified?
sections.description: Diagnostic criteria and grading based on support needs (DSM-5 approach).
sections.content:
In current clinical classification, ASD is evaluated under a single “spectrum” diagnosis. The diagnosis is made through expert observation and caregiver information regarding the child's/individual's development, behaviors, and functioning.

According to DSM-5, two main areas stand out in the diagnosis of ASD:
1) Persistent difficulties in social communication and interaction
2) Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior/interests and excessive adherence to routines (including sensory responses)

A “severity/level” specification can be made based on support needs:
- Level 1: Requires support
- Level 2: Requires substantial support
- Level 3: Requires very substantial support

Additionally, the following co-occurring conditions are specified:
- Language development (with/without accompanying language impairment)
- Intellectual development (with/without accompanying intellectual disability)
- Known medical/genetic conditions and co-diagnoses (e.g., ADHD, anxiety, epilepsy)

Note: Some sub-diagnoses previously known by separate names (e.g., Asperger's, etc.) are now considered within the ASD spectrum.

sections.title: What Are the Causes of Autism Spectrum Disorder?
sections.description: There is no single cause; genetic and environmental factors play a role together.
sections.content:
There is no single proven cause of ASD. Scientific evidence shows that genetic factors and some environmental/biological factors together can increase the risk of ASD by affecting early brain development.

Known general framework:
- Genetic factors: A family history of ASD and some genetic syndromes can be associated with risk.
- Environmental/biological factors: Some pregnancy and birth-related factors (e.g., advanced parental age, prematurity, some birth complications) have been associated with risk.

Important information:
- There is no reliable scientific evidence that vaccines cause ASD.

Note: A “risk factor” does not mean that something definitely causes ASD; it may simply be found to be probabilistically associated. The causes are not the same for every child and family.

sections.title: What Are the Symptoms of Autism Spectrum Disorder?
sections.description: Social communication and repetitive behavior patterns; sensory differences.
sections.content:
Symptoms vary from person to person; however, differences in two main areas are typically seen in ASD.

1) Difficulties in social communication and social interaction
- Difficulty initiating and sustaining reciprocal communication
- Difficulty using or understanding nonverbal cues such as eye contact, gestures/facial expressions
- Difficulty making and maintaining peer relationships

2) Restricted and repetitive behaviors / interests
- Repetitive movements or play patterns (e.g., rocking, lining up objects)
- Excessive adherence to routines, intense difficulty with changes
- Intense and restricted interests
- Differences in sensory responses (over- or under-reacting to stimuli such as sound/light/touch)

Some children may experience a plateau or regression in development (especially in communication skills). It is important to consult a specialist if such changes are noticed.

sections.title: The Importance of Early Diagnosis and Early Education
sections.description: Early intervention can provide significant benefits in communication, social skills, and daily life.
sections.content:
Early diagnosis allows the child's developmental needs to be understood earlier and the right supports to begin sooner.

Why is it important?
- Early intervention services (especially in the preschool period) can be effective in developing the child's communication, social interaction, and learning skills.
- Family guidance and home modifications (visual supports, routine planning, creating communication opportunities) make daily life more sustainable.
- Co-occurring difficulties (sleep, nutrition, anxiety, attention, etc.) can be noticed earlier and appropriate referrals can be made.

Practical steps
- Tracking developmental milestones and requesting an evaluation if in doubt
- Evaluation in fields such as child development / child and adolescent psychiatry / pediatric neurology
- Regular work with individualized goals in services such as special education and speech-language therapy

Note: The best program is one that is individualized according to the child's strengths and needs.
